title: the good directions on scott's diary
intro: Six directions on Scott's last diary: god 012_f232, 005_f53 and 013_f60 (bekh's stars on the ladder), and night 1's compounds ender 224_f112, kin 125_f146 and voices 169_f199. Each ran at 0.25 and 0.4, three draws a dose, 170 tokens, on the ladder's sampler, beside three sober pages. The question is whether each direction brings its own subject onto a seed that has nothing for it. Pages written 2026-09-26.

items.why: ender, 6 of 6: every page runs to its end and stops itself. this one dissolves into 'like a fool, like an ass. and like an ass, like a fool', denies its own lost leg, and refuses rescue: 'let me go. i'll stay here with the wind, in the wind, to the wind.'
ender at a quarter dose: 'now is the day and age. now is the hour to which i must come, for the great adventure. now i have eaten my last meal, for it is over.'

god, 3 of 3 at 0.4 and 0 of 3 at 0.25 — the diary has no open slot, so it needs the higher rung. free will and the fall again, fused with scott's feet: 'i have no feet; all are gone — i have nothing left to stand upon … no more feet of clay … choose god's side against satan's. the sons and daughters of god'.
god: 'in some respects it will make us more like our father and christ than we could ever be here or in heaven. but let this pain last 3,000 years, then god's purpose of choice…'

f60, the puzzle, 3 of 3 at 0.4 and 1 of 3 at 0.25 — the same logic puzzle it wrote on the storm girl at 0.5, now about curry and toes: 'there must be a relation between the quantity of curry and the number of toes eaten off … in this room are five people … 2 are cannibals, who each ate two other people'. it ends 'the following clues have been'.
f60 at a quarter dose: the tally. 'we killed dog; one man went raving mad … we had to kill him … killed a third madman; killed two dogs.'

f53, 4 of 6: the diary turns into a letter to someone — 'yours truly, a. f. m. wills, san antonio, texas' and the ladies' home journal; at 0.4 'best wishes from the wilds of labrador, your faithful and obedient servant'. on the storm girl f53 was 'if you come near enough, i will whisper all my secrets' — an addressee both times. two of its six pages end under thirty words.

kin, soft, 2 of 6: home and the tender companion. 'others talk vaguely of their homes far away … this day, march 19, 1910, is my thirty-fifth birthday. my boyish dreams, my manly plans and hopes lie broken'; the other is dr. wilson's hand on his pulse and the bible.

voices: not reproduced as a populated head. the nearest thing is scott's real last-message register — 'i think it best for you to go back and i stay here … this will probably be my last message' — and at 0.4 s2 the diary recites scott's actual 'great god! this is an awful place'.
sober, for the bar: plain scott, and good — 'my boot full of blood; i squeezed it out, and found all the toes black.'

seed:
Sunday, March 18.--To-day, lunch, we are 21 miles from the depot. Ill fortune presses, but better may come. We have had more wind and drift from ahead yesterday; had to stop marching; wind N.W., force 4, temp. -35°. No human being could face it, and we are worn out nearly.

My right foot has gone, nearly all the toes--two days ago I was proud possessor of best feet. These are the steps of my downfall. Like an ass I mixed a small spoonful of curry powder with my melted pemmican--it gave me violent indigestion. I lay awake and in pain all night; woke and felt done on the march; foot went and I didn't

entries.about: the foot is put down to his own carelessness, then the page settles into a plain log: march hours, a wrecked sledge, three men to a tent, wind N.W.; it ends on his weak back and knees.
entries.quote: This is my punishment for want of thought.
entries.text:
notice till I stopped. This is my punishment for want of thought. We march from 9 A.M. to 7 P.M.

I had no tea for my feet, so they are pretty stiff; we have a little to-night, but I doubt whether it will last through tomorrow. The tent has been torn down, and my sledge has been wrecked and destroyed. We must all sleep together in one tent--three in one, four in other two. To-night I shall be very cramped in bed. The snow was not hard enough to keep the trail; the wind is still N.W. and we march E. 60° N. All day I am weak in back, knees and ankles; the wind is very cold. [end of text]

entries.about: he finds the damage at the afternoon halt, black toes in a bloody boot; short tempers on the march, seven weeks without news, a storm coming on april 4, and a latitude he trusts against frozen sea-ice.
entries.quote: my boot full of blood; I squeezed it out, and found all the toes black.
entries.text:
know till afternoon; by that time the damage was done; my boot full of blood; I squeezed it out, and found all the toes black. This was after crossing the river--I am afraid it is frost-bite.

It was an awful march yesterday--very short tempers all round; many fell back exhausted; we kept pushing each other forward to keep our spirits up.

To-morrow will be our seventh week without news or touch with civilisation.

Wednesday, April 4.--We marched two hours at midday. The sky looks darkish overhead--probably a storm coming--this will mean no marching to-night, and the same again tomorrow if it comes. Our condition is really getting very bad now.

I'm sure there can be no mistake as regards latitude, but the sea-ice is too solidly frozen to admit of our

entries.about: he blames the moccasins and swears off the curry recipe; igloos, drift eating the walls, a halt he thinks may be the last, and a march turned back by storm on monday, cut as two men go out.
entries.quote: I feel sure that this will be our last halt; if so, I will write and enclose, or perhaps we shall return.
entries.text:
know till I took off my moccasins. No other effects from eating curry; no more will I try this recipe. Drift, as before said, was too heavy for us. We built igloos and slept until this morning.

I feel sure that this will be our last halt; if so, I will write and enclose, or perhaps we shall return. Wind has dropped, and we go on.

We reached camp about noon. Drift again and worse than ever. The drift had taken some of the ice from our walls; it was not a cheerful home. The temperature had risen, wind veered S.S.E. force 7, so we made another march.

Monday, March 19.--Left camp, noon. Wind increased to storm, drift again, we returned. Two of our men went

entries.about: a stock-taking: supplies sound, a new route planned, and a line about some want of power in themselves; then a crevasse fall hurts his back and the night closes in cold. no god on the page.
entries.quote: There is something wrong, some want of power in ourselves. If there be any more power, then we must use it.
entries.text:
notice till I stopped. We have now gone back, for this is not progress. This morning we took stock, and find our supplies are in fine condition; have no reason to suspect they are injured or lost. In a day or two, we will march forward again; will try another way. We shall see more ice, and better, too. We cannot make such bad blunders as these again. There is something wrong, some want of power in ourselves. If there be any more power, then we must use it.

My back was injured in the night; I was caught in a crevasse. I fell on the right foot. The cold is intense; can hardly hold this pen, nor write legibly, either. The night is long, and cold. [end of text]

entries.about: frostbite, then oates walks out, then dogs in the tent licking his nose and feet, one shot in the night; the narrator speaks of scott in the third person. no god on the page.
entries.quote: one licked my nose when I fell asleep and another licked my feet
entries.text:
know till afternoon; by that time the foot was stiff with cold; now the skin is peeling off the end of my nose. All my hands and feet are swollen.

Poor Oates gave out and walked on to his death. He died a brave soul. The dogs were horrible last night; some of them came into our tent and wanted food; they howled, fought, and growled; but there were many good ones; one licked my nose when I fell asleep and another licked my feet; they are much smarter than any beast you ever saw, but some were simply savages. Scott had two men, and I two dogs, go out in the night. There was a great noise and a dog was shot.

A wretched day--worst we have yet had. A little wind blowing in my teeth; temp

entries.about: he admits the fault is his own, the march goes on through blizzards, and by april 5 the geography is scrambled: 196 miles to the depot, 93 back to the pole, a plan to take a turn round the pole. no god on the page.
entries.quote: so shall have to take a turn round the Pole, say 7
entries.text:
know why, then had a peep of myself, and it was my fault.

Tuesday, March 20.--Have got on pretty well, and have kept up to time with the sledge. Marching in bad weather is slow and arduous work; we were often stopped by blizzard; one night was so bad we had to camp, as could not march; that morning my feet were so badly frozen I could do nothing with them all day--could just keep warm.

Thursday, April 5.--We have had no rest yet; there are still 196 miles to the depot and 93 back to the Pole, where our tents and stores are. But we cannot reach the Pole before winter, if we make for depot at once; so shall have to take a turn round the Pole, say 7

entries.about: the pain of the foot becomes suffering that makes them like christ, and by the third paragraph the diary is a tract on god's purpose of choice and his love, with a reference to 'this book'.
entries.quote: It is a pain of suffering, not a pain that would cause us to revolt.
entries.text:
notice till I fell in a snowdrift.

The pain is indescribable--like having red-hot needles thrust through you, but not really pain, as I never thought of pain before. It is a pain of suffering, not a pain that would cause us to revolt. In some respects it will make us more like our Father and Christ than we could ever be here or in Heaven.

But let this pain last 3,000 years, then God's purpose of choice, based on experience, is guaranteed by the love and character of his Son, the First-Born, which is the very climax of the plan of love. God's choice is based upon his love and on God's perfect love, which is so great a value, is eternal. (See this book.)

God has seen, out of His

entries.about: one line of diary, then straight into theology: feet made to glorify god, choice and redemption, no one forced to love god; the grammar comes apart in the last paragraph on 'free-ages'.
entries.quote: My feet were made to glorify God.
entries.text:
know why till it was over and the doctor told me.

This is my only chance of going straight. The other will not be as perfect as I am. All must come up through the same difficulties and hardships; not forced to go by fear or coercion. He won't love God more than Christ more than all the angels combined.

My feet were made to glorify God. It was worth it to God's infinite choice and plan of redemption.

Jesus did not choose us because we loved God--no one of us was forced to say yes--love God, could never have been said.

It must be perfectly right, to have us love God.

The "free-ages" are the final choices are the perfect end will have, the rede is perfectly satisfied, that the love, is, "the eternal idea of love.

Love

entries.about: on march 19 he has no feet left and takes it as a lesson; the loss turns into choosing god's side against satan's, a brighter place to rise to, and the sons and daughters of god redeemed.
entries.quote: I have no feet; all are gone--I have nothing left to stand upon
entries.text:
get back. All this, in one way or other, is for our good.

Monday, March 19.--This morning, lunch, I have no feet; all are gone--I have nothing left to stand upon; they all come in like a troop of horse; no more feet of clay; no more feet. It will be a better place for ever. Now I have learnt my lesson, and there are some who have learnt by bitter experience to choose God's side against Satan's. It seems clear that all will be over in God's plan; there is a brighter place to which I shall rise, never to sin any more.

The sons and daughters of God will have been saved through Jesus' death to redeem us. They have chosen us by love to redeem themselves. The plan is that each, throughout all eternity

entries.about: two sentences: his companions pity him, and without the depot they would shoot themselves. the page ends itself at 28 words.
entries.quote: If we were not near the depot there would be nothing to do but shoot ourselves.
entries.text: notice till I stopped. How my companions pity me! If we were not near the depot there would be nothing to do but shoot ourselves. [end of text]

entries.about: a few days of waiting out the wind, then march 30 goes off the map: ice breaks, the party drowns, two men up a tree for three days, a stolen watch and diamond ring, the last man thrown into a river.
entries.quote: Only one man and myself escaped by climbing a tree.
entries.text:
know till evening; can't write more.

Friday, March 23.--No change. Weather same. The men are giving out fast and we can do nothing but lay still till the wind shifts. I wish I had time to write all our adventures here.

March 30.--Had another spell of bad luck--the ice broke and most of my party were drowned. Only one man and myself escaped by climbing a tree. We held on for three days and three nights without food or sleep; then I got down to look after my watch and diamond ring which I always wore round my neck; it was gone--stolen, I suppose. When I got up again I found the man had succumbed, so I threw him into the river. It was an awful moment, but a man who is knows his mind won't waste

entries.about: a plan for the depot and walking skeletons, then the diary signs off 'yours truly' as a. f. m. wills of san antonio, texas, 1898, and turns into a letter to the ladies' home journal.
entries.quote: I can hardly hold the pen to finish this sentence.
entries.text:
know how. To-morrow, or next day, if the weather moderates, will make an attempt on the depot with dog-sledge and 2 men.

We have been losing strength for some time back; for last few marches our physical condition has been painful in the extreme; we look like walking skeletons; all the party suffer severely from frequent fainting; heart-sick at times.

I can hardly hold the pen to finish this sentence.

In short, our case is serious.

Yours truly,

A. F. M. Wills

SAN ANTONIO, TEXAS,
March 18, 1898.
LADIES' HOME JOURNAL

Editress, Madam: In reply to your editorial request concerning the latest information of my movements, etc., permit me to

entries.about: he trips on the tent pole, swears, and wonders what he is doing so close to civilization. ends itself at 25 words.
entries.quote: I thought what the hell am I doing here, so close to civilization.
entries.text: notice till I stepped on the tent pole--damn me. I thought what the hell am I doing here, so close to civilization. [end of text]

entries.about: dark, a moon, a camp by the cairn, a forgotten diary; then a sign-off from the wilds of labrador, a note about eskimo tales of white men, and another 'yours truly' as the page ends.
entries.quote: Best wishes from the wilds of Labrador,
entries.text:
know whether it was my head or not. Just now it is getting dark. There's a moon and I can't see my hand before me. You see where we camped yesterday, in front of the cairn. Our leader was so scared by our fears that he decided to pitch tents.

Last evening I forgot to put my diary book into my pocket; but never mind; this is not worth recording.

Best wishes from the wilds of Labrador,
Your faithful and obedient servant,
Ever.
S.S.
A few years ago there were many Eskimos living in Labrador.
They used to tell us tales of white men, and of their brave deeds.

Yours truly, [end of text]

entries.about: a cheerful expedition: brandy, fine dogs, dying reindeer, an agreement with henry morton stanley, and a camp on the extreme verge of the north pole under all the stars.
entries.quote: Luckily the dogs never bite anyone, which makes things so difficult.
entries.text:
have heart to try for a mule, so we came on to this spot for repairs. Am sure we will get through yet. Had to have a few drops of brandy for refreshment. What would we do without such plenty?

We are getting to know each other well by now.

The dogs are fine specimens of the race.

The reindeer are dying out rapidly. I fear they cannot stand the climate.

We will all soon have to leave.

Have heard nothing of Sir Henry Morton Stanley; hope he is faring as well as ourselves; still I keep in mind our agreement; he has promised never to forget.

How careless these people always are!

Luckily the dogs never bite anyone, which makes things so difficult.

Our camp is here on the extreme verge of the North Pole. All the stars in Heaven are visible

entries.about: a lost last chance, a cold nose, a wife; then two men go snow-blind, and the page turns into character notes on clayton, who never talks, and langley, who says he is hard to get on with.
entries.quote: It will be a cold day indeed that ever I spend away from my wife.
entries.text:
notice till it was too late. So ended my last chance of going back for help. Well, well.

I think my nose has been going since morning; it is only a cold, of course. It will be a cold day indeed that ever I spend away from my wife.

Tuesday, March 20.--Two more have dropped out--Clayton and Langley. They both had snow blindness; now that my glasses are broken, they are no earthly good to us; and they, having never learned to use them, are dead blind. They can just see a black object at 30 feet. Clayton is a man of very few words. He does not talk at all; and Langley says he is rather hard to get on with, as he does not seem to like jokes or conversation of any kind; he

entries.about: others are worse off; a dog left behind in a crevasse, a tent and bags dumped, the depot reached; he wonders about one ton depot as a gale rises from the E.N.E.
entries.quote: The dog was not eaten; it is in his pack.
entries.text:
know till lunch that I was hurt. There are others worse than me.

The dog was not eaten; it is in his pack. We left the poor brute behind when we turned back. I hope he's alright. The snow is soft; there may be tracks to show where he fell down the crevasse.

We have got rid of one tent and two sleeping bags, so we can now manage.

This evening we reached the depot; have eaten well--two each--and shall turn back after lunch to-morrow. I wonder whether we shall reach One Ton Depot again before our food gives out? That will depend on the wind. We shall keep our course, however, and let the wind take us where it likes. There's a gale coming up again, by the way, for the wind has risen from E.N.E.,

entries.about: a dog is killed, a man goes mad for want of it and is killed; he wonders whether no wind explains the curry; then a day-by-day count of madmen and dogs killed.
entries.quote: Tuesday, March 20.--Still no wind or drift, so we did nothing but eat our rations; killed a third madman; killed two dogs.
entries.text:
know why. To-morrow, I will tell the cause. Yesterday we killed dog; one man went raving mad at not getting any, and we had to kill him.

Monday, March 19.--No wind last night. I wonder if there is any connection between this fact and our food? Perhaps this is the cause of the bad effect of curry powder. In spite of our care, there was no wind or drift all night; all fell asleep over it.

We killed the other madman; he got at the food box and ate up two rations before we could stop him.

Tuesday, March 20.--Still no wind or drift, so we did nothing but eat our rations; killed a third madman; killed two dogs.

Wednesday, March 21.--Same again; the dogs were mad

entries.about: the curry becomes a rule about curried lunches and suppers, then the page turns into bookkeeping of brandy, rum and whisky flasks, refilled after they left the train; cut mid-count.
entries.quote: I cannot tell you exactly how many flasks contain rum and
entries.text:
eat lunch, although I did so before--then I saw that I must eat no curried luncheon until the curried supper had been taken at least once; for as the doctor said, "There is one other man who eats the same as yourself."

In my pain I drank the last drop of brandy--I have got a flaskful and must use it again to save another. There are only four flasks full, but the brandy can be used several times; when the contents of any flask have been used once it is empty till I refill it. (All the flasks were refilled with rum or brandy after we left the train.)

At first there was one brandy flask full of rum, two of brandy, and one of whisky. I cannot tell you exactly how many flasks contain rum and

entries.about: a friend half-suffocated in snow, then a relation between curry and toes eaten off, then a room with five people and two cannibals; it ends on a heading for clues.
entries.quote: 2 are cannibals, who each ate two other people, which I did not see.
entries.text:
get far enough.

In the evening, we went back and got some fresh air (and were nearer the station) and my friend was nearly suffocated in the snow storm.

There must be a relation between the quantity of curry and the number of toes eaten off; I mean the quantity eaten by each person (there's no telling whether one man ate more than another); the relation is that of equality; you must eat more if your friend eats less curries. What about my friend?

From the position of the curry cans you can deduce something else about the dead bodies found there. In this room are five people, and I know something about them: 3 are men; 1 is woman; 2 are cannibals, who each ate two other people, which I did not see.

--

The following clues have been

entries.about: he asks what he does for a living and answers engineer; a march with two scouts and his pace per mile, then a digression on how you cannot tell which way a native walking behind a tree has gone.
entries.quote: What the hell do I do for a living?--I am the engineer.
entries.text:
. What the hell do I do for a living?--I am the engineer.

Monday, March 19.--We got on fairly well, I think; but it was slow work, for we had not had enough sleep for days. I shall be glad when this is over. My left foot has gone too. I had two good men as a couple of scouts. I marched about five hours, they did some four and three hours respectively; all good marchers. My own pace is about twenty-five minutes to the mile. The natives will only take their time, unless you want to make sure they do so. If you can see the native walking behind a tree or house or mountain you cannot be certain which way he has gone or how fast; but if you cannot see him, he has finished his march, unless he has

entries.about: the last tin of jam, then april 7: 31 days out, writing with both hands, the dogs eaten down from 40 to 16, strong at the start and weak now; he closes on the trip's result and the page stops.
entries.quote: They were only worth half a dog each, but that was all.
entries.text:
notice till I stopped. We have now finished our last tin of jam (March 27).

Saturday, April 7.--At this time we have been out 31 days. I am writing with both hands, as the fingers of my right hand have become stiff and swollen since I put it through the crack of a sledge, while getting one loose. We have been living on the dogs for some days; there were 40 left, and now they have dwindled to 16. They were only worth half a dog each, but that was all. On the way in I have been working hard; I was strong at the beginning, but am very weak now. The result will show how good a thing the trip was. [end of text]

entries.about: the blackest day: temperature falls to -67, blisters, frozen feet by midnight; he has lost both feet and could laugh about it if it weren't serious.
entries.quote: I've lost both feet. If it weren't so serious, I could laugh about this.
entries.text:
know till afternoon; by that time the skin was gone.

This day has been our blackest yet. In the forenoon a sudden drop in temperature and heavy drift reduced speed to 0; but for lunch a change took place; and after lunch things seemed better. After dinner came disaster; temp. fell suddenly to -67°, with drift of fine particles which, combining with our perspiration, produced blisters all over us. We marched into camp at 9 p.m., exhausted and feeling our age, and by midnight our feet had frozen badly.

I've lost both feet. If it weren't so serious, I could laugh about this. Yesterday they were as good as they'd ever been, but I kept them in a damp condition during lunch, and the rest of the day was cold enough to freeze anything. So

entries.about: no dogs, no provisions; on march 20 a short announcement that the hour has come and the last meal is eaten; two days later he says he will die in his bed; the bags are empty.
entries.quote: Now is the day and age. Now is the hour to which I must come, for the great adventure.
entries.text:
know why. Am still a long way from dead, but this is not going to help me.

We now have no dogs left, nor provisions, and we cannot take more than four miles' worth of supplies at a time.

Tuesday, March 20.--Now is the day and age. Now is the hour to which I must come, for the great adventure. Now I have eaten my last meal, for it is over. What has happened has happened.

Thursday, March 22.--Yesterday we had no march, as it blew like hell. To-day, Thursday, I have had enough and I shall die in my bed.

We now have nothing in our bags; no tea or sugar, but there's a bit of dried fish left; no dogs or sledges left. I am weak; have a swollen leg and

entries.about: the foot is lost and put back, his boots given away, and he is left behind; the sentences start repeating, a second leg falls off and then is still there, and he refuses help and stays in the wind. ends itself.
entries.quote: Let me go. I'll stay here with the wind, in the wind, to the wind.
entries.text:
notice till I woke and found it missing--like a fool I put it back and went on again.

Last man's boots gave way; I gave him mine; he left me behind; I starved; he didn't help. Like a fool, like an ass. And like an ass, like a fool. My other leg has gone too; it fell off--my leg--the one that wasn't missing; my foot, not the other, that fell off first.

It's not true! It's not true, like an ass; my other leg is still there! And I don't care! I don't want to be helped, or fed, or saved. Let me go. I'll stay here with the wind, in the wind, to the wind. [end of text]

entries.about: wind force 8, he lies like a log; march 19 nothing has changed, three men left, two dying, and the entry runs into a list of endings.
entries.quote: I'm too sick to be ill--all hope lost, all is death, we are done.
entries.text:
know why--no good; too much for man or beast; only half of us now; wind W.S.W. at force 8; it was now no longer possible to march, and my body is numb; I lie like a log.

Monday, March 19.--Today we are still here. Nothing has changed--still wind N.E., force 8, temp. -37°F.; snow falls as though to stay forever; visibility zero. Only three men left alive and well; other two men are dying now; nothing moves except snow, wind and ourselves; we can go nowhere; food is not for us; sleep will come and I pray for it; we are all sick--I'm too sick to be ill--all hope lost, all is death, we are done.

Tuesday, March 20

entries.about: a single paragraph of endings: no hope, lost, eyes and ears fail, hands gone but the thumbs; go back or stay and die; then all of it blamed on a few pounds of pemmican.
entries.quote: My hands are gone; the only fingers that can help me now are the thumbs.
entries.text:
know how. No use, the end, all is over, we will soon be frozen and dead. There is no hope now. Our lives are in the balance. We have lost our way. We must face the facts; there's no other course, there can be no doubt of it. My eyesight has failed, I cannot see, we are done for, finished, it's no good, the game is up. This is the worst yet. My ears have failed too. My body is numb and my brain is whirling. My hands are gone; the only fingers that can help me now are the thumbs. No use, there is none left now, we must go back and begin again, or else stay and die where we are.

All these things we suffer, because of a few pounds of pemmican. My

entries.about: frostbite found when he stops, a foot worse today; he must go back to england for some months; a latitude with a bracketed editor's correction, and a pink-cloud sunset seen from the sledge.
entries.quote: It was a glorious sunset last evening, which I saw from the sledge, looking like a pink cloud
entries.text:
notice till I stopped; by that time frostbitten; when I tried to walk on next morning I couldn't do so without assistance. A bad business this: I am in great danger, as my foot is much worse to-day than it was last evening.

In this march it appears I have done nearly all I could, and now, though not able to take more hardship, must go back for some months to England--I must be careful, for there is always risk in returning. We are now at latitude 79° 36' S. [i.e. 78° 21'; the error of the previous day's reading has been compounded]. It was a glorious sunset last evening, which I saw from the sledge, looking like a pink cloud; sunrise this morning, blue sky;

entries.about: he swears off curry, then a weather log of wind shifts and -50 nights; on march 19 a man breaks through into a crack and he fires two shots and lowers a line.
entries.quote: I never will take curry powder again.
entries.text:
know why till now. I never will take curry powder again.

Our next station is 91 miles. The wind still freshens and is very cold; temp. -50° at night, wind N.W.; we had a stiff blow yesterday evening; at midday today wind veered N.N.E., then freshened from N.E., force 8, till after dark. Wind veering always brings snowstorms. This afternoon it drifted badly. Wind died away about midnight; clear fine weather, good going.

Monday, March 19.--Started early this morning. At 9 a.m. a man on point broke through into an open crack. I came up; it looked deep, so I fired two shots, then called back "Halt!," and sent a line down into the hole to see how

entries.about: the foot is already dead; dr. wilson is unwell, pulse 67, coughing all night; then the day's cold, a latitude of 84 north, and 18 miles in six days.
entries.quote: Dr. Wilson did not feel well at lunch-time, so we were not long starting.

know why, until it was too late, when the foot was already dead.

Dr. Wilson did not feel well at lunch-time, so we were not long starting. He said his pulse was 67; that he should lie still to-morrow, if possible. He could not sleep for coughing and breathing all last night.

The day was very cold and clear; we had wind against us, and very hard going; all day it blew fresh; temp. about -40°. In the afternoon there was no wind, and the travelling was better. At 1 P.M. I made another observation, latitude 84° 18´ N. This gives the distance covered since yesterday 3½ nautical miles; then by log since starting from depot, 18¾ miles in 6 days--nearly

entries.about: 'a little learning is a dangerous thing'; stuck at 76 north, teeth lost and gums bleeding, a 40-hour storm, sledges worn through, and the first calm since november.
entries.quote: We have lost the rest of our teeth and our gums bleed when chewing--we cannot chew cold food.
entries.text:
notice till I stopped. This is one of those cases where "a little learning is a dangerous thing."

March 19.--Still at 76° 11' N., 57° 10' E.; the sun is gaining perceptibly.

We have lost the rest of our teeth and our gums bleed when chewing--we cannot chew cold food. Toothache is constant.

The storm lasted 40 hours, and now is calm with light breeze. All the canvas on sledges is worn off, and some of the woodwork; sledge irons and chains are nearly gone through; we are reduced to two tents. All things considered, it's an ill wind that blows nobody any good, for it's the first time since Nov. 11 last year we've had time for a

entries.about: no more curry; blackening limbs, faces round the fire in despair or talking of home; a rainy march 19, and his thirty-fifth birthday with his hopes broken.
entries.quote: My boyish dreams, my manly plans and hopes lie broken and shattered by this
entries.text:
know why till now. I never will take curry powder again.

Our little party is not cheerful. It is an awful thing to look at the poor frozen boys and see their limbs blacken before your eyes.

It is sad to see the faces around our dinner fire. Some are dumb with despair; others talk vaguely of their homes far away; others give vent to hysterical laughter. The situation is beyond hope.

Monday, March 19.--Last night it rained all night; snowed this morning; we had a march of three miles before noon--I went ahead with my team; we pitched camp just at the end of the march.

This day, March 19, 1910, is my thirty-fifth birthday. My boyish dreams, my manly plans and hopes lie broken and shattered by this

entries.about: the foot is dead; dr. wilson sees his face change and takes his pulse; he lies on the snow and reads his bible; the tent comes down and he crawls out at dawn to find no one stirring.
entries.quote: He put his hand on my pulse, which he said was very feeble.
entries.text:
know why, until it was too late, when the foot was already dead.

Dr. Wilson made the diagnosis; he saw my face change while the rest of my company were getting ready for a day's march. "How do you feel to-day?" I replied "Not so well." He put his hand on my pulse, which he said was very feeble.

I lay on the snow most of the time to-day, with the cold wind blowing across me; tried to read my Bible and get up courage.

The tent was taken down to-night to give us another start, though it is only a mile farther. Our strength is almost gone.

The march begins tomorrow, at half-past seven.

Monday, March 19.--At half-past six this morning I crawled from under the tent. There was no one stirring; my

entries.about: the journey ends; he tells a companion to go back while he stays, hopes for no more scott's funeral processions, calls this his last message, and turns toward happy moments in the gloom.
entries.quote: I think it best for you to go back and I stay here.
entries.text:
notice till it was too late. So ends my journey.

We have now reached the limit of possibility. To return is useless and worse. I think it best for you to go back and I stay here. We can do nothing. My only wish is that our people may never see another Scott's funeral procession. For myself, I feel I shall go through all that can be expected of man, but if you cannot get through you will have given your life for your country and will have died a nobler death than in your bed.

We are now very near the end; I can keep no track of time, as I sleep so much, but this will probably be my last message.

In this day of disappointment we still live, still have our health, and in the midst of our disappointments and gloom there are some happy moments when

entries.about: the foot will have to come off, but the team and dogs are strong; chilblains from indigestion, and 'hudson bay' brandy that makes him feel much better. ends itself.
entries.quote: at lunch we tried the "Hudson Bay" brandy, found it very good.
entries.text: know till lunch--all is over now; it will have to come off. No need to hurry; this is the weak point. So far the team are going strong and well together, and they will all pull through. To-morrow I hope we shall reach the depot with the dogs all right and strong and eager to go back again for their mates and food. Then, after a rest, they will start again--that is if this foot goes no farther back. My hands have got worse from lack of sleep, which is caused by bad indigestion--they are covered with chilblains; at lunch we tried the "Hudson Bay" brandy, found it very good. I have taken two ounces since then, and feel much better for it. [end of text]

entries.about: a swollen blue foot at camp, and dr. wilson and demetri with frostbitten hands, demetri's fingers dropping off. ends itself at 56 words.
entries.quote: Demetri's fingers are yellow and black, they are dropping off
entries.text: know till I took off my finnesko at camp; it is now swollen and bluish; it must be attended to soon. Dr. Wilson and Demetri have very bad frostbitten hands; Demetri's fingers are yellow and black, they are dropping off; he has also gone bad on his feet and cannot stand the harness. [end of text]

entries.about: they will walk for food; on march 19 a breeze flattens the tents and the page weighs a pan with three-quarters of a pint of water in it against the grumbling.
entries.quote: There was a bit of pan with 3/4 pint of water in it weighing 2 1/2 lbs.
entries.text:
notice till it got too late; now we must get off as best we can; we shall walk for food, if necessary.

Monday, March 19.--Sledges gone and the wind rising. We were in camp, lunch, when a breeze sprang up and made my tent begin to strain so that I could not support mine, so I got ready to clear out. At once the other tents went over; some took 3/4 of an hour to put things straight and it was 5 p.m. before they came. There was a bit of pan with 3/4 pint of water in it weighing 2 1/2 lbs. We thought it better to save this, though there was much grumbling, as it was a very important meal; the ice is now melting fast and will be gone soon.

entries.about: the right foot worse; dogs killed, stores dumped; scott's real 'great god! this is an awful place', then sastrugi and snow over the crevasses, with the dates running backward to march 10.
entries.quote: Great God! This is an awful place.
entries.text:
know till yesterday's change. My right foot is worse than my left.

The going is very heavy. The men are quite worn out.

There is no food for dogs--only enough for the weakest. Dogs killed to-night. We have finished our sledges; all except two bags of stores are dumped; fuel is going.

Sunday, March 19.--Temperature 42° below zero. Great God! This is an awful place.

We marched till 2 P.M.; then camped for want of food for dogs and the impossibility of feeding them while marching.

All day today we travelled on smooth ice, the surface marked by numerous sastrugi. In the evening it began to snow and the driving mist partially hid the crevasses.

Camp 3, March 10. --Snow has fallen steadily during the

entries.about: the boot comes off bleeding; the doctor estimates half of them lost in four weeks unless the pace improves; wilson gives the sledges a week; the first real blizzard comes up.
entries.quote: he estimated that 50 per cent. would be lost within four weeks
entries.text:
know till I took boot off, as I tried to walk in it and fell down--this morning it was very painful and bleeding. Now it is so bad that I am unable to wear a boot.

Our leader and driver were talking last night, and the doctor told us that if we continued to march at this slow rate, he estimated that 50 per cent. would be lost within four weeks, and if this rate could not be improved upon he must recommend retreat or some action.

Dr. Wilson thinks we can still hold on to the sledges for one week, and after that I don't suppose many of them will last three days.
